This number can reduce unwanted oscillations of the wheel that arise due to latency, although too large a number can introduce jerkiness into the force output.

There is a delay between the time the simulation calculates the forces you should be feeling and the time the device actually makes you feel them. This number attempts to compensate for that delay by predicting what the forces will be this many milliseconds in the future. Finding the right number is largely a matter of feel. The steering can be made to feel more immediate, but too large a number can introduce jerkiness into the force output.

The various driving aids are intended for novice players as well as for those players without analog controls.  NOTE: In Hardcore Mode Multiplayer races, some driving aids may be disabled for all participants.

If checked, equips your car with an anti-lock braking system.  While anti-lock brakes make the car easier for the novice driver to control, the experienced driver will be able to brake more efficiently with this option turned off. NOTE: If braking has been assigned to a button or a key rather than a controller axis, this aid will be turned on by default. Otherwise, the car would be very difficult to control while braking.
If checked, equips your car with an automatic transmission. The automatic transmission shifts more slowly than its manual counterpart, resulting in slower lap times for the experienced driver.

If checked, equips your car with an automatic clutch. While the manual clutch can provide greater shifting precision, it requires proper heel and toe downshift technique and therefore is recommended only for experienced users. The manual clutch is not available if Automatic Shifting has been selected.

If checked, equips your car with automatic steering assistance. With the steering assistance turned on, it is more difficult to spin the car. This aid is particularly useful for novice drivers and for those who are steering with buttons or the keyboard, but disabling it will provide greater steering precision. NOTE: If the steering has been assigned to buttons or keys rather than a controller axis, this aid will be turned on and cannot be turned off. Otherwise, the car would be very difficult to control.

If checked, equips your car with a traction control system. While traction control makes the car easier for the novice driver to control, the experienced driver will be able to accelerate and corner more efficiently with this option turned off. NOTE: If the throttle has been assigned to a button or a key rather than a controller axis, this aid will be turned on be default. Otherwise, the car would be very difficult to control while accelerating.

If checked, equips your car with a magical device that tries to help the car to not get too sideways. While this makes the driving experience less frustrating for a novice driver, the experienced driver will be able to corner more efficiently with this option turned off.

Ratings are based on a 1-100 scale, with 50 being average. Prior to each race, a driver's rating in a given category is randomly generated between its MIN and MAX values specified below. Use the arrow controls to edit a rating. Altering these ratings can produce dramatic changes in behavior and therefore is recommended only for advanced users.
Patience level when attempting a pass or blocking. High aggression may increase the chance of driver error.
Ability to run consistent laps. Note that it is possible to be consistently SLOW. Consistency also affects the chance of driver error.
The ability to finish a race well. Drivers with a high Finishing rating will get stronger as the race nears its end.
Overall performance in Qualifying sessions only.
Overall performance on tracks under one mile in length.
Overall performance on ovals between one and two and a half miles which do not mandate the use of a restrictor plate.
Overall performance on ovals of two and half miles and over, including those at which a restrictor plate is mandated.
The ability of the car to slip through the air with a minimum of drag. A higher Aero rating means less drag, which translates to more speed.
Chance for a mechanical failure. Higher reliability translates to a lower chance of such an occurrence.
The more consistent the pit crew is, the less likely a mistake will be made during a pit stop.
A high rating translates to quicker times for all pit operations: changing tires, adding fuel, making setup adjustments, and repairing damage.

A measurement of the team's willingness to take pitting risks in order to gain track position. This can be done in several ways, the most obvious of which involves taking none or two tires rather than four. As this value increases, the team becomes more willing to take such chances. Because of this fact, a high Strategy rating isn't necessarily better than a low one.
Track selection area. The arrow controls cycle alphabetically through the tracks one at a time, while the list box control displays the names of all available tracks.
If checked, eliminates the Practice and Happy Hour sessions from the race weekend.

Multiplies the tire wear and fuel usage rates by the indicated value.  1x translates to normal usage, 2x double, 3x triple, and 4x quadruple usage.  This option is useful for setting up a short race which normally would not require a pit stop.

Displays an overhead view of the car along with its weight at each of the four corners.
More forward weight increases stability for high-speed cornering and braking. More rear weight permits the car to rotate around slow, sharp corners more quickly.
For ovals, all possible weight should be moved left.  For road courses, centered weight or even full right weight may be preferred.
More cross weight, or wedge, will make a car tighter.  Less will make it looser.

The qualifying engine gives more power, but will tend to overheat if used for more than a few laps. The race engine is designed to go the full race distance. You are automatically given the qualifying engine in a qualifying session, and the race engine in a happy hour or race session. In practice or testing you are free to try either.

The differential gear ratio is used to adjust all four gears together. A smaller ratio allows for higher top speeds, but produces less torque at the rear wheels, so it will take longer to reach top speed.

A taller gear (smaller number) is better for higher speeds.  A shorter gear (larger number) is better for strong acceleration.  Select gearing such that the car accelerates briskly through gears 1-4, and that the engine RPM tops out around 9,000 (7,000 at the restrictor plate tracks) in top gear.

This is the number of engine revolutions for each revolution of the rear wheels in the given gear. This allows a meaningful comparison of gear ratios when changing both the diff ratio and transmission ratios.
More grille tape reduces drag and increases front downforce, making the car turn better.  More tape also makes the engine run hotter.
A steeper rear spoiler increases drag and rear downforce, making the car tighter.  A flatter spoiler reduces both, and makes the car looser.

Lower tire pressures result in a more forgiving car, and higher tire temperatures. Higher pressures allow higher top speeds with less temperature buildup. The recommended pressure will keep the middle (M) temperature on the tires near the average of the inside (I) and outside (O) temperatures. Going higher than recommended can result in more speed at a high-speed track, but the loss in grip can hurt at slower tracks.

At the RF shock, adding compression (higher number) will tighten the car on corner entry, while less will make it looser.  For the LF, adding compression will loosen the car on corner entry, while less will tighten it.  For the RR, adding compression will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will make it tighter.  For the LR, adding compression will tighten the car on corner exit, while less will make it looser.

At the RF shock, adding rebound (higher number) will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will tighten it.  For the LF, in high-speed corners adding rebound will loosen the car on corner exit, while less will tighten it.  In low-speed corners, the exit effect will be reversed.  For the RR, adding rebound will tighten the car on corner entry, while less will loosen it.  For the LR, adding rebound will loosen the car on corner entry, while less will tighten it.

Increasing RF spring stiffness will tighten the car, particularly on corner entry.  Softening it will have the reverse effect.  Increasing LF can make the car turn better on corner entry, but may tighten it in the remainder of the corner.  Increasing RR will make the car loose, particularly mid-corner and on exit. In high-speed corners, aerodynamic effects may overcome this.  Increasing LR will make the car tighter on corner exit, but may loosen it in mid-corner.
Adding negative camber on a right side tire (or adding positive camber on a left side tire) increases lateral grip on that tire, up to a point.  Excessive camber can greatly increase tire wear.

Adding positive caster 'removes wedge' from the car as the tires are steered, making the car looser.  Unequal caster (caster split) imposes unbalanced forces on the steering system that the driver can feel.
Raising the track bar loosens the car. Increasing the split (running higher right side than left side) loosens the car under power and in high-banked corners, and tightens it under braking.

Increasing the ride height will increase the car's ground clearance.  The car's body position will remain unchanged.  Higher ground clearance may be desirable at tracks with higher banking in order to prevent the car from 'bottoming out' in the corners.
If the car doesn't turn well under braking, decrease the front brake bias. If it wants to spin under braking, increase the front bias. Go with the lowest front bias you can control.

Roll couple can be thought of as the car's weight bias as it's cornering. Displayed as percentage front. Roll couple is not directly adjustable; its value is derived from your spring and sway bar settings. Increasing roll couple will tighten the car and promote understeer, while decreasing it will loosen it and promote oversteer.
Increasing front toe-out settles the car in a turn, but too much can produce understeer. 1/8 inch toe-out is a very common setting.
Increasing front bar size will make the car tighter while cornering.
Increasing rear bar size will make the car looser while cornering.

This list shows which replay editing operations are active.  To change or remove an operation, click on the appropriate info line to select it, and then click the EDIT or DELETE button at the bottom of the list.
Lets you make changes to the selected operation.  NOTE: Camera switches and chapter breaks cannot be edited, but they can be deleted.
This list contains ready-made artwork that you may find useful.  To use one of the items, click on its information line to select it, and then click the INSERT button at the bottom of the list.
Places the selected resource into the replay.
Speed, Gear, Throttle, and Brake data for the selected driver.  Throttle and Brake information is available only for the local player driver.
Rewinds to the start of the replay.
Rewind control.  If the replay is already rewinding, each successive press of this button will increase the rewind rate.
Rewinds one frame per click.  If held, the result will be a slow, steady rewind.
Pauses the replay if it is in motion.  If the replay is paused, pressing this control initiates forward playback at the normal (1x) rate.
Advances one frame per click.  If held, the result will be a slow, steady advancement.
Fast forward control.  If the replay is already advancing, each successive press of this button will increase the advance rate.
Advances to the end of the replay file.

Places a marker at the current frame of the replay.  Only one marker can exist at a time, so pressing the button again will move the marker to the new location.  You must place a marker in order for the Cut, Copy, and Paste functions to work.
Cut.  Deletes footage from the marker to the current frame.  A pop-up box will tell you how many frames of footage were cut.
Copy.  Copies footage from the marker to the current frame up to the clipboard.  A pop-up box will tell you how many frames of footage were copied.
Paste.  Pastes footage copied to the clipboard into the replay at the current frame.  Existing footage is pushed forward in time to resume at the end of the copied section.
Saves the edited replay file to your REPLAY folder.

Changes the car being viewed.  In replays from Multiplayer races, not all cars may be visible at all times.  Keyboard shortcuts: V (next car), Shift - V (previous car), Ctrl - V (switch to local player's car).
Changes the camera view.  Keyboard shortcuts: C (next camera), Shift - C (previous camera).
Takes you to the previous/next point in the replay at which this function was used.
Inserts a custom piece of artwork into the replay.  Artwork files must be in .BMP or .TGA format (toggle using the button to the right) and must reside in the EXPORTS/IMPORTS folder.
Inserts a sound clip into the replay.  Sound files must be 22kHz 16bit in .WAV or .OGG format (toggle using the button to the right) and must reside in the EXPORTS/IMPORTS folder.
Inserts a text bubble into the replay.
Inserts a fade effect into the replay.  Fades are useful for covering up heavily-edited portions of a replay that may look awkward otherwise.
Inserts a camera switch into the replay.  Use the camera controls above to select the angle you want, then press this button.
Inserts a car switch into the replay.  Use the car controls above to select the driver you want, then press this button.
Changes the speed of the footage so that you can add effects like slow motion and dramatic pauses to your replay.

Changes the volume of the game sounds (NOT custom sound clips) in the replay.  This is useful if you want to play a sound clip while the replay is using a particularly loud camera angle such as the cockpit view.

Designed for those who wish to create their own Driving Lessons, this function places a chapter break in the replay.  Chapter breaks make it easy for those using the lesson viewer to navigate among the different sections of a replay file.  To view a replay file in the lesson viewer, copy it to the LESSON subfolder of the main program.
